summary: Defines terminology for the behaviors of NATs handling unicast UDP and sets requirements so applications like voice, video and online gaming work consistently through them. This is a Best Current Practice.

plainLanguage.summary: Network Address Translators (NATs) can handle the same UDP traffic in different ways. RFC 4787 describes these behaviors and sets rules intended to help applications communicate through NATs more consistently.

subtitle: A common set of rules for how NATs handle unicast UDP traffic.

tldr.problem: NAT devices handle UDP differently, making it hard for applications such as multimedia communication and online games to work consistently.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC names specific mapping and filtering behaviors and sets requirements for port assignment, timers, hairpinning, ICMP, and fragmented packets.
tldr.outcome: NATs that meet the mandatory requirements are compliant with this specification. RFC 4787 is a Best Current Practice updated by RFC 6888 and RFC 7857.

sections.title: The Problem and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 4787 sets behavioral requirements for traditional Network Address Translators (NATs) handling unicast User Datagram Protocol (UDP) traffic over IP. It aims to make applications such as multimedia communication and online games work more consistently.

NAT behavior varies, so an application cannot easily predict how traffic will cross a particular device. The RFC defines shared terms and rules for NAT behavior. It does not specify general firewall behavior, UDP relays, or application behavior.

The RFC avoids older broad labels such as Full Cone and Symmetric because they did not describe real NAT behavior well. It describes individual mapping and filtering choices instead.
sections.plainLanguage: A NAT changes network addresses, but devices can handle UDP in different ways. This RFC gives NAT makers shared terms and rules so applications can better predict what the device will do.

sections.title: How NATs Map Addresses and Ports
sections.content:
When an internal device starts an outgoing UDP session, the NAT assigns an external IP address and port. The NAT uses this mapping to translate traffic between the internal and external endpoints.

With Endpoint-Independent Mapping, traffic from the same internal address and port uses the same external mapping for any destination. With Address-Dependent Mapping, the mapping is reused only for the same destination IP address. With Address and Port-Dependent Mapping, it is reused only for the same destination IP address and port. REQ-1 requires Endpoint-Independent Mapping.

If a NAT chooses an external address from a pool, Paired pooling keeps an internal address associated with the same external address. REQ-2 recommends this when pooling is supported, helping applications that use multiple ports from one internal address.
sections.plainLanguage: A NAT gives an inside device a public address and port for sending UDP traffic. RFC 4787 requires it to keep that same mapping when the device contacts different destinations.

sections.title: Ports, Mapping Timers, and Address Conflicts
sections.content:
REQ-3 forbids port overloading, where a NAT assigns the same external port to conflicting sessions. It recommends keeping a translated port within its original range: 0-1023 or 1024-65535. REQ-4 recommends preserving whether the port is even or odd.

A mapping timer controls how long a mapping stays active without traffic. REQ-5 says it MUST NOT expire in less than two minutes, with an exception for specific applications using well-known destination ports (0-1023). A default of five minutes or more is recommended. REQ-6 requires outbound packets to refresh the mapping; inbound packets may refresh it.

REQ-7 covers NATs whose external address is configured dynamically. They must prevent their internal and external address ranges from conflicting, or translate traffic correctly even when addresses overlap.
sections.plainLanguage: A NAT must not give two active sessions the same outside port. It must also keep a UDP mapping for at least two minutes, except for the stated port-specific case, and refresh it when inside traffic is sent.

sections.title: Filtering and Hairpinning
sections.content:
Filtering controls which incoming packets can use an existing mapping. Endpoint-Independent Filtering allows packets from any outside source to reach the internal endpoint. Address-Dependent Filtering allows packets only from IP addresses the endpoint contacted. Address and Port-Dependent Filtering also requires the outside port to match.

REQ-8 recommends Endpoint-Independent Filtering when application compatibility matters most, or Address-Dependent Filtering when stricter filtering matters more. The administrator may be given a choice.

Hairpinning lets two devices behind the same NAT communicate using each other's external addresses. REQ-9 requires hairpinning, with the forwarded packet showing the sender's external address and port.
sections.plainLanguage: Filtering determines which outside senders can reach an inside device. Hairpinning lets two devices behind one NAT contact each other through their public addresses, and the forwarded packet must show the sender's public address.

sections.title: Gateways, ICMP, and Fragmented Packets
sections.content:
Application Level Gateways can rewrite UDP-based protocols and interfere with NAT traversal or integrity protection. REQ-10 says these gateways SHOULD be off, and recommends that administrators be able to enable or disable each one separately.

A NAT is deterministic if its mapping and filtering behavior do not change without a configuration change. REQ-11 requires deterministic behavior. REQ-12 says receiving any ICMP message MUST NOT end a mapping; the default configuration SHOULD NOT filter ICMP based on source address, and support for Destination Unreachable messages is recommended.

For outgoing packets with the Don't Fragment bit set, REQ-13 requires the NAT to return an ICMP message if fragmentation is needed. If the bit is clear, the NAT must fragment the packet. REQ-14 requires handling fragments that arrive in order or out of order, while ensuring fragment-based denial-of-service attacks do not prevent normal packet processing.
sections.plainLanguage: The NAT should avoid rewriting UDP traffic with application gateways and must not end a mapping just because an ICMP message arrives. It must also handle fragmented packets without letting fragment attacks block ordinary traffic.

sections.title: Compliance, Security, and Current Status
sections.content:
A NAT that meets all mandatory requirements is compliant with the specification. A NAT that also meets the recommended requirements is fully compliant. Applications may not know whether a NAT meets these rules, so the RFC says peer-to-peer media applications still need normal procedures such as Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE).

The RFC notes that inbound packets refreshing a mapping can let an outside attacker keep it active indefinitely. Out-of-order fragment handling also requires stored state, which can create denial-of-service risks if implemented poorly. Endpoint-Independent Mapping itself does not change which packets pass through; filtering controls that decision.

The document is a Best Current Practice for traditional NATs handling unicast UDP. The unit metadata records that RFC 6888 and RFC 7857 update it.
sections.plainLanguage: A NAT follows this specification when it meets the required rules; meeting the recommended rules makes it fully compliant. RFC 4787 is a Best Current Practice and was updated by RFC 6888 and RFC 7857.

viz.caption: SUMMARY OF THE FOURTEEN NAT REQUIREMENTS

items.label: RECOMMENDED
items.desc: Use Paired address pooling when pooling is supported.

items.label: MUST NOT
items.desc: Expire UDP mappings in under two minutes, with a stated exception.

items.label: MUST
items.desc: Avoid or handle internal and external address conflicts.

items.label: RECOMMENDED
items.desc: Choose a filtering behavior based on the desired balance.

items.label: MUST
items.desc: Support hairpinning with the external source address and port.

items.label: MUST
items.desc: Keep mapping and filtering behavior deterministic.

items.label: MUST NOT
items.desc: Terminate a mapping when any ICMP message arrives.

items.label: MUST
items.desc: Handle outgoing packets according to the Don't Fragment bit.

items.label: MUST
items.desc: Receive in-order and out-of-order fragments safely.
